topics.name: Authentication & Identity Basics
topics.key_points: Authentication binds principals to actions; authorization governs permitted actions; audit records actions. Principal classes: humans/machines authenticating each other (passwords, biometrics, tokens, CAs). Attribute = property of a principal; identity = set of attributes; identifier = attribute unique within a population. Authentication checks an identity against known attributes (vs. identification = finding someone in a crowd). Enrollment: establishing identity with a system; verification of claimed attributes varies (websites rarely, governments often).

topics.name: Human-to-Machine Authentication Factors
topics.key_points: Three categories: something you are (biometrics: fingerprint, retinal scan), something you know (password, PIN, security questions), something you have (key, ATM card, token). Two-factor authentication = two independent methods (ATM card + PIN); multi-factor = 2+. Combine separate categories; two passwords are not independent factors.

topics.name: Passwords: Creation and Strength
topics.key_points: Password lifecycle: create, store, use, change/reset. User-chosen passwords are often guessable (top 20 passwords compromise ~10% of accounts); system-generated ones are unmemorable. Strength: if 2^X guesses needed, strength is X bits. For length L over alphabet N: entropy X = L·log2(N). Shannon entropy poorly predicts real crackability since humans pick non-uniformly (random word from 50k vocabulary ≈ 16 bits).

topics.name: Password Storage, Hashing, and Salts
topics.key_points: Threat model: offline attack (attacker reads disk/memory). Store uid, H(p) — need deterministic, one-way, collision-resistant hash. Attacks: identical passwords yield identical hashes; dictionary attacks precompute common hashes; rainbow tables. Defense: per-user random public salt; store uid, s, H(s,p). Unsalted brute force over M passwords and N users is O(M+N); salted is O(MN). Pepper is an alternative (see reading).

topics.name: Online Attacks, Rate Limiting, and Slow Hashes
topics.key_points: Online attack: adversary interacts as a user. Don't leak valid usernames (ask both in parallel, don't reveal which failed — Failsafe Default); log failures (Defense in Depth); lock accounts, rate limit. Slow hashes (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2) add large constant factor hurting attackers, not users. PBKDF2: iterate HMAC ~10,000s of times with password+salt; output usable as symmetric key. Slow down fast hashes by iterating and XOR-combining.

topics.name: Access Control Model and Protection Domains
topics.key_points: Access control policy: relation Auth over principals × objects × operations (matrix). Reference monitor mediates every operation ⟨P,O,op⟩; assumptions: predefined operations are sole info channels and all can be monitored (complete mediation). DAC: owner defines authorizations; MAC: central authority. Principles: Failsafe Defaults (enumerate privileges, not prohibitions), Least Privilege (fine-grained). Protection domains: threads carry privilege sets, transition via system calls; attenuation = losing, amplification = gaining privileges.

topics.name: ACLs, Capabilities, and Confused Deputy
topics.key_points: ACL encodes matrix column (per object: list of ⟨principal, privs⟩): easy per-object review, simple revocation, but slow per-principal review and vulnerable to confused deputy. Confused deputy: server tricked into using its own privileges on client's behalf (writing results to charges.txt passed as f). Fix: capabilities — unforgeable (name+privilege) bundles combining naming with authorization. Capability list encodes row (per principal). C-lists stored in kernel memory; Unix file descriptor table is an example. Capabilities: no confused deputy, but review/delegation/revocation are hard.

topics.name: Mandatory Access Control: MLS, Bell-LaPadula, Biba
topics.key_points: MLS: labels L = (sensitivity, compartments); sensitivity Unclassified ≤ Confidential ≤ Secret ≤ Top Secret; compartments enforce Need-to-Know. L1 ⊑ L2 iff S1 ≤ S2 and C1 ⊆ C2 (partial order; some labels incomparable). BLP (1973): no read up (simple security: S reads O iff L(O) ⊑ L(S)); no write down (*-property: S writes O iff L(S) ⊑ L(O)) — provably prevents laundering/Trojan horses. Issues: blind writes, attenuated logins, declassification via trusted subjects. Biba (1977): same rules for integrity (Trusted ⊑ Untrusted). SELinux implements MAC/MLS. Other MAC: Brewer-Nash, Clark-Wilson, RBAC.

topics.name: Block Cipher Recap & ECB Mode
topics.key_points: Block cipher: k-bit key, n-bit block, E(K,M) bijective and indistinguishable from random permutation without key (AES standard). Raw block ciphers are deterministic so not IND-CPA and only encrypt n bits. ECB mode: split M into blocks, encrypt each independently with same key; deterministic => not IND-CPA (penguin image leaks structure).

topics.name: CBC Mode
topics.key_points: Cipher Block Chaining: Ci = EK(Mi ⊕ Ci-1), C0 = random IV; ciphertext is (IV, C1...Cm). Decryption: Mi = DK(Ci) ⊕ Ci-1. IND-CPA secure if IV is random and never reused. Encryption sequential, decryption parallelizable. Needs padding to block multiple (PKCS #7: pad with number of padding bytes, full dummy block if already aligned). IV reuse leaks common prefix blocks.

topics.name: CTR (Counter) Mode
topics.key_points: Simulates one-time pad: compute pad = EK(nonce || counter) per block, XOR with plaintext; only uses block-cipher encryption. Ciphertext (nonce, C1...Cm). Both encryption and decryption parallelizable; no padding needed. IND-CPA if nonce never reused; nonce reuse is catastrophic like OTP key reuse (leaks plaintext). Best for high performance.

topics.name: IVs, Nonces & Mode Comparison
topics.key_points: IV: random, public, one-use value adding randomness; in CTR called nonce (number used once) — must be unique, not necessarily random; terms used interchangeably. Never reuse: CBC reuse leaks partial info (equal prefix blocks), CTR reuse is catastrophic. Theory: CBC and CTR equally secure if used properly; CTR for performance, CBC if paranoid about misuse.

topics.name: Lack of Integrity/Authenticity in Block Ciphers
topics.key_points: Block cipher modes give confidentiality (IND-CPA) only; tampering isn't detected. CTR bit-flipping attack: knowing M, Mallory computes pad byte Padi = Mi ⊕ Ci, then sets C'i = M'i ⊕ Padi to change 'Pay Mal $100' to '$900' without the key. In CBC, flipped bits turn a block into gibberish but receiver can't tell it wasn't sent — still no integrity/authenticity.

topics.name: Public-Key Cryptography Overview
topics.key_points: Each person has a key pair: public key known to everyone, private key secret. Based on number theory (modular arithmetic, factoring, discrete log) vs symmetric XORs/bit-shifts; messages are numbers, not bit strings. Benefit: no pre-shared secret needed between Alice and Bob. Drawback: much slower than symmetric crypto.

topics.name: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
topics.key_points: Public: large prime p (2048-bit), generator g. Discrete log problem: given g, p, g^a mod p, finding a is hard. DH assumption: can't distinguish g^ab mod p from random given g^a, g^b. Protocol: Alice sends g^a mod p, Bob sends g^b mod p; shared key K = g^ab mod p. Weaknesses: vulnerable to MITM (Mallory substitutes g^m), needs both parties online, no authentication (fixable with digital signatures; ElGamal addresses some issues).

topics.name: RSA Encryption & Hybrid Encryption
topics.key_points: KeyGen: pick large primes p,q; N = pq (2048–4096 bits); choose e relatively prime to (p-1)(q-1) with 2 < e < (p-1)(q-1); d = e^{-1} mod (p-1)(q-1) via Extended Euclid. Public key (N,e), private key d. Enc: C = M^e mod N; Dec: M = C^d mod N. Security: RSA problem no harder than factoring N (assumed hard). Hybrid encryption: encrypt random symmetric key K with asymmetric crypto, data with symmetric — fast for large messages; used in almost all systems.

topics.name: Side channels among implementation weaknesses
topics.key_points: Implementation is often the weak link. Threat taxonomy: bugs (buffer overflows); fault injection = active, partially invasive (e.g. Row-hammer); side channels = passive, non-invasive attacks that observe byproducts (time, power, EM, sound, temperature, accelerometer) rather than breaking the algorithm.

topics.name: Information flow security & non-interference
topics.key_points: High (secret) vs low (public) variables; explicit flows (public=secret+1) and implicit flows (if secret>0 then public=1) violate security. Non-interference: s1~s2 (same low values) implies program(s1)~program(s2). Declassification (=declass) relaxes it, e.g. PIN check reveals only (input==pin). IND-CPA game formalizes this: attacker picks two low-equivalent states, one is run with p=1/2, any poly-time attacker wins with prob at most 1/2+negligible.

topics.name: Timing side channels
topics.key_points: Formally: even if program(s1)~program(s2), executions remain distinguishable via observation channels. PIN check with early-exit loop leaks correct prefix: brute force needs avg 5K of 10K combos (3 guesses ~3/10000), timing reduces to 10 worst-case per digit, avg 5 (3 guesses ~1/1000). Non-time channels exist too: auto-increment DB ids leak row counts (register/bid examples).

topics.name: Cache architecture & cache attack types
topics.key_points: Caches are transparent, shared, have collisions; misses cost more time; 64-byte lines, eviction with write-back if dirty. Attack types: time-driven (measure victim exec time to estimate hits/misses, e.g. >1 miss implies Secret!=0); access-driven (probe shared memory, or prime+probe all 64 lines and time reloads); trace-driven (profile cache activity per operation, e.g. Miss-Miss-Hit vs Miss-Hit-Miss reveals branch); instruction-cache attacks. Practical problems: noise from other processes, multiple accesses per line.

topics.name: Access-driven attack on AES
topics.key_points: AES: symmetric cipher, 128-bit key brute force infeasible (264 billion years at 1 decryption/us). Last round: C[j] = T(B[i]) XOR K[j], SBox T is a 256-entry lookup table. Attacker model: controls plaintext, observes ciphertext, knows T, shares cache; goal is finding SBox index i to get K = C XOR T[i]. SBox = 1KB = 16 lines of 16 entries; ~1000 encryptions suffice. Small example C = M[P]+K demonstrates candidate-set narrowing from observed cache lines.

topics.name: Non-elimination key recovery method
topics.key_points: L = log of (ciphertext c, accessed lines e). L(j,v) = entries with c[j]=v; since c[j]=K[j] XOR T[i] with T a permutation, all elements of L(j,v) share a line. E(j,v) = intersection of their line sets; P(j,v) = T{E(j,v)} = candidate SBox values. Shrink with v1 XOR v2 = T[i1] XOR T[i2] across two values. When |P(j,v)|=1, K[j] = v XOR P(j,v)[0]. Repeat per byte, no new logs; ~850 encryptions, under 1 second.

topics.name: Countermeasures
topics.key_points: Eliminate: disable caches (huge perf cost); flush cache at entry/exit; cache partitioning/coloring via MMU (even/odd pages per process - under-utilizes cache); victim actively evicts/normalizes SBox lines, or waits to Worst Case Execution Time. Reduce bandwidth: add noise (random data accesses/computations), reduce timer precision. Randomize data position (&M'= &M+r), layout (M[pi(i)]), and code order. Detection: spot priming (suspicious lines at context switch) and probing (frequent time syscalls). Constant-time programming: never branch on secret, secret-independent memory accesses (e.g. branchless modular exponentiation for RSA).

topics.name: Other side channels
topics.key_points: Browser fingerprinting: passive/active collection of User-Agent, screen, fonts, plugins, audioContext etc.; >80% of 4M+ fingerprints unique, ~90% attributes stable over months; enables cross-site tracking without cookies. Mitigations: Brave/anti-fingerprinting, common defaults, VMs. Network analysis: DASH video identification from chunk sizes/timing (BPS/BPP features + CNN), up to ~0.985 accuracy even sniffing LTE radio. SSH: inter-keystroke packet timings reveal typing patterns and passwords; defenses: buffering/coalescing keystrokes, traffic shaping.

topics.name: Course Overview & Organization
topics.key_points: DD2395/DD2391/DD2394; lecturers twice weekly, in-person. Labs: GPG secure email (Lab G), web attacks (Lab W), buffer overflow (Lab O), optional zip bomb (Lab Z). Merit points can raise exam grade B/A. Written exam Oct 19, re-exam Dec 16. Soft vs hard deadlines; code of honor and AI policy; breaking into others' systems is criminal.

topics.name: Defining Security
topics.key_points: Computer security = how systems behave in presence of an adversary (intelligence actively causing misbehavior). System is secure when it 'does what it should and nothing more'. Security policy stipulates what should/shouldn't be done, specifies what not how (e.g. 'prevent theft of money'). Principal = entity that can take actions (person, program, system), distinct from principle.

topics.name: Security Properties: CIA Triad
topics.key_points: Confidentiality: protection of assets from unauthorized disclosure (privacy concerns info about individuals). Integrity: protection from unauthorized modification; output correct per specification. Availability: protection from loss of use; DoS affects availability. Examples: copying homework violates confidentiality; freezing a system violates availability.

topics.name: Attacker's vs Defender's Mindset
topics.key_points: Attacker: find ways security can break, weakest links, question assumptions security depends on, think outside the designer's worldview. Defender: know what you defend and against whom; risk analysis; benefits vs costs (no system is completely secure); 'rational paranoia'. Common mistake: convincing yourself the system is secure — instead identify and fix weaknesses.

topics.name: Security Model Components
topics.key_points: System model (how system behaves; trace models, PL-semantics models), security policies (CIA + privacy, accountability), threat/attacker model (what attacker can observe — output, timing, power — and influence; attacker may supply code or be co-resident), trust, mechanisms, assurance. Bear-race parable: 'good enough' defense suffices to redirect attackers elsewhere.

topics.name: Trust, TCB, and Assurance
topics.key_points: Trust = expected behavior of a principal (an assumption). Trusted Computing Base (TCB): components whose failure compromises security (e.g., SSH daemon, OS, CPU; not a video app). Trustworthy = evidence it satisfies policy. Assurance asks whether mechanisms enforce policies — reduce system security to TCB security; keep TCB small (KISS: Keep It Simple, Stupid); formal reasoning and testing.

topics.name: Security Mechanisms & Strategies
topics.key_points: Countermeasures neutralize threat or vulnerability. Strategies: Prevent (block attack), Deter (make harder), Deflect (make other targets attractive), Mitigate (lessen harm), Detect (during/after), Recover (undo harm). Mechanisms: cryptography, authentication, access control, isolation, sandboxing, monitoring, information flow control, security testing, fuzzing, dynamic/static analysis, verification.

topics.name: Security Principles
topics.key_points: Accountability (authentication, authorization, audit = 'Gold Standard'); Complete Mediation (reference monitor intercepts every operation, part of TCB); Least Privilege (minimum privileges needed); Failsafe Defaults (default 'no', allowlists > denylists); Separation of Privilege/Duty (require collusion); Defense in Depth (overlapping mechanisms, Theodosian Walls); Economy of Mechanism (small TCB); Open Design (no security through obscurity, assume attacker knows all); Psychological Acceptability (unusable security gets bypassed; warning dialogs signal failure; social engineering).

topics.name: What is Cryptography
topics.key_points: Older def: secure communication over insecure channels. Newer def: rigorous guarantees about data and computation in presence of an attacker — not just confidentiality but also integrity and authenticity. Never write your own crypto; use well-vetted libraries. Goal: become a good consumer of cryptography.

topics.name: Cast of Characters & Three Goals
topics.key_points: Alice/Bob communicate over insecure channel; Eve = eavesdropper (honest-but-curious, passive); Mallory = manipulator (malicious, can read and modify). Three goals: Confidentiality (adversary can't read messages), Integrity (adversary can't change messages undetected), Authenticity (prove message origin). Integrity is prerequisite for authenticity.

topics.name: Keys, Encryption & Integrity Mechanisms
topics.key_points: Attacker knows all algorithms (principle of open design); only the key is secret. Symmetric model: shared secret key. Asymmetric: public + secret key pair. Confidentiality via encryption: plaintext + key -> ciphertext -> decrypt. Integrity via tag/signature (seal analogy): tampering invalidates the tag; Bob verifies it.

topics.name: Threat Models
topics.key_points: Models classified by Eve's power: ciphertext-only (no trickery), chosen-plaintext (can get encryptions of chosen messages), chosen-ciphertext (can get decryptions), chosen plaintext-ciphertext (both — strongest and defensible in practice). Lecture focuses on the chosen-plaintext (CPA) model.

topics.name: Symmetric-Key Encryption Definition
topics.key_points: Three algorithms: KeyGen() -> K; Enc(K, M) -> C; Dec(K, C) -> M. Messages are bitstrings. Required properties: correctness Dec(K, Enc(K, M)) = M; efficiency (fast on standard computers); security = confidentiality. Encryption alone does not provide integrity or authenticity.

topics.name: IND-CPA Security Definition
topics.key_points: Game-based definition: Eve queries encryptions of chosen plaintexts, submits equal-length M0/M1, challenger encrypts Mb for random b, Eve queries more, then guesses b. Scheme is IND-CPA secure if every polynomial-time Eve wins with probability <= 1/2 + negligible epsilon. Insecurity = some strategy wins with probability > 1/2.

topics.name: Edge Cases: Length, Runtime, Negligibility
topics.key_points: Schemes may leak message length (hiding it is impractical; apps can pad); hence M0/M1 must be same length. Eve limited to polynomial runtime. Negligible advantage ~ O(1/2^k) for k-bit key: 1/2^128 negligible, 1/2^20 not; ~2^80 a reasonable current threshold but changes over time — know your threat model.

topics.name: One-Time Pad
topics.key_points: XOR review: x⊕0=x, x⊕x=0, commutative/associative. OTP: KeyGen = random n-bit key (n = message length, fresh per message); Enc(K,M)=K⊕M; Dec(K,C)=K⊕C. Correctness: K⊕(K⊕M)=M. Perfectly secure (win probability exactly 1/2) since random K makes both plaintext hypotheses equally likely. NOT IND-CPA secure: key reuse lets attacker query Enc(K,M0) and compare.

topics.name: Security Protocols: Purpose & Threat Model
topics.key_points: Protocols embed crypto primitives in structured message sets to remove trust in the channel (voting, signatures, auth email, blockchains). Threats: address spoofing, eavesdropping (Eve), malicious principals (Bob). Protocol design is subject to subtle errors.

topics.name: Secure Bank Transfer Case Study
topics.key_points: Build up iteratively: digital signatures prevent spoofing; replay attacks countered by nonces (bank checks Log/DB) or timestamps (accept 1 tx per 5s, reject older). Include recipient in message (else reusable for other receivers/banks) and acknowledgements (else sender can't detect dropped/altered messages).

topics.name: Common Attacks & Desired Properties
topics.key_points: Attacks: known-key, replay, impersonation (person-in-the-middle), reflection (replay to original sender, typical with shared keys). Properties: confidentiality, authentication, integrity, freshness (this run, not replay), explicitness (this protocol, not copied from another), forward secrecy (key leak must not compromise past messages).

topics.name: Protocol Design Guidelines
topics.key_points: Every message contains a nonce; replies include the nonce replied to plus a fresh one. Messages explicitly name sender and intended recipient. Messages specify the protocol, its version number, and the message number within the protocol instance.

topics.name: Digital Certificates & Trust Models
topics.key_points: Certificates bind a public key to a subject, signed by a CA (may include validity, authorization, timestamps). Chain of trust: CA2 certifies CA1, etc.; root certs are self-signed and blindly trusted (e.g. Chrome root chain). Web of Trust: decentralized; users hold key rings and sign keys of trusted users; deferred trust via signature verification.

topics.name: Session Key Exchange & Denning-Sacco Flaws
topics.key_points: Public-key crypto is expensive, so parties negotiate a symmetric session key via a trusted CA. Denning-Sacco [DS81] flaws (Abadi & Needham 1994): message reuse lets Bob impersonate Alice; reflection attacks; key derivation attack (Bob infers K+1 used with Eve); compromised forward secrecy — one leaked key exposes all previous messages.

topics.name: TLS: Handshake & Key Derivation
topics.key_points: TLS gives confidentiality, integrity, server authenticity over in-order TCP; used in HTTPS, SMTP (STARTTLS), VPN. Handshake: client sends 256-bit RB + cipher list; server sends RS, chosen algorithms, certificate; client sends premaster secret PS encrypted with server public key (proves private-key ownership). Both derive keys CB, CS (encryption) and IB, IS (MACs) from RB, RS, PS; MACs over handshake detect tampering; fresh RB/RS per connection prevents replay.

topics.name: TLS Attacks, Bugs & Formal Verification
topics.key_points: Downgrade/P(M)ITM: force export-grade ciphers (e.g. 512-bit RSA from 1990s US export rules), solve DLP/RSA problem, recover plaintext — 8.5% of top 1M sites vulnerable (2015). OpenSSL Heartbleed (memory safety). Apple 'goto fail' bug skipped certificate checks enabling impersonation. Verification: Tamarin symbolic models (abstracted crypto, attacker capabilities; can miss unstated assumptions like nonce reuse) vs EasyCrypt computational model (probabilistic reductions to hardness assumptions).

topics.name: Web Application Security Landscape
topics.key_points: Modern web apps are complex: page code, ad code, 3rd-party libs, frames, extensions. They handle sensitive data (financial, health, personal) wanted by hackers, insurers, ad companies, governments. Many acting parties: page/library developers, service/data/ad providers, CDNs, network providers. Goal: build flexible, secure apps from untrusted components.

topics.name: HTTP Protocol, URLs and Cookies
topics.key_points: HTTP is an application-layer protocol for fetching resources via URL (scheme://domain:port/path?query#fragment). Request/response messages; methods: GET (no state change), POST (creates/updates), PUT, PATCH, DELETE. HTTP is stateless; cookies are server-sent data the browser stores and echoes back, used for session management, personalization, and tracking (Set-Cookie header).

topics.name: Browser Execution Model, DOM and JavaScript
topics.key_points: Browser loads root page, parses HTML, runs JS, fetches subresources, responds to events (onClick, onLoad, setTimeout). Pages can nest frames/iFrames from different sources; browser provides frame-based isolation. DOM is an OO interface letting JS read/modify page content; JavaScript is client-side, embedded via <script>, runs in the browser with the page's privileges.

topics.name: Same Origin Policy (SOP)
topics.key_points: Attacker models: network attacker and web attacker (evil.com). Origin = (scheme, domain, port) triple; SOP isolates origins for confidentiality and integrity. Separate SOPs exist for DOM, CSS/fonts, cookies. Frames access only same-origin data; postMessage/CORS relax SOP with explicit mediation (check event.origin). Scripts/images can load cross-origin but run with the page's privileges.

topics.name: Cookie Scope and Cookie Security Flags
topics.key_points: Cookie SOP uses (scheme, domain, path), not port. A page can set cookies for its own or parent domains (not public suffixes); without Domain attribute the cookie is host-only. Browser sends cookies whose domain is a suffix of URL domain and path a prefix of URL path. Flags: HttpOnly hides cookie from JS (document.cookie); Secure = HTTPS only; SameSite=Strict = sent only for same-site requests.

topics.name: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
topics.key_points: Attacker page triggers requests (e.g. or auto-submitted form) that carry the victim's auth cookies; attacker can't read the response but state changes happen anyway — cookie-based auth is insufficient for side-effecting requests. Defenses: secret per-session validation tokens in forms, Referer/Origin header validation, SameSite cookies.

topics.name: SQL Injection (SQLi)
topics.key_points: Occurs when SQL queries are built by string-concatenating user input, e.g. "SELECT id FROM users WHERE username = '$login'". Attacks: alice' (syntax error), '--' (comment), ' or 1=1 -- (bypass login, matches all users), '; drop table users -- (damage). Defense: never build SQL yourself — use parameterized/prepared queries where values are sent separately from the command (also faster via cached query plans).

topics.name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and CSP
topics.key_points: XSS: untrusted data sent to browser without validation/sanitization; attacker's code runs in victim's browser (vs SQLi on server). Types: reflected (script reflected in page, e.g. search?q=<script>...), stored (saved in DB; Samy worm on MySpace via CSS javascript: URL), client-side/DOM XSS (insecure default browser APIs like document.write on location.href). Blacklist filtering is hard (~105 event handlers, encodings, <scr<scriptipt evasion). Defenses: proper escaping, frameworks, and Content Security Policy (e.g. default-src 'self'; script-src allowlist, blocks inline scripts).

topics.name: Memory bugs & Rowhammer
topics.key_points: Memory bugs enable: secret data access, data corruption, unexpected control transfer, access violations, attacker-chosen code execution. Rowhammer: DRAM cells interact electrically; repeatedly reading (hammering) one line can flip bits in another — usable from JavaScript to flip JIT code/pointers. Defenses: ECC memory, physical separation on DRAM.

topics.name: Compile-time prevention: safe languages & coding
topics.key_points: Strongly-typed high-level languages block untyped memory access; Rust uses ownership/borrowing to enforce lifetime rules without GC. Costs: performance, memory, timing predictability; guarantees rely on correctness of unsafe components. Safe C coding: check buffer capacity, validate lengths (integer overflow), handle allocation failures, define ownership/lifetime, mind null terminators; strncpy() may leave buffer unterminated.

topics.name: Static analysis, formal verification & testing
topics.key_points: Static analysis finds defects without executing code; formal verification proves properties mathematically — a proof is a guarantee under explicit assumptions (cost ~$2000/LOC 2010, ~$500 2020). Verified platforms: seL4 separation kernels, ARMor software fault isolation, Frama-C. Testing: fuzzing, symbolic execution (solve path constraints), Memcheck tracks addressability and definedness; passing tests never proves absence of defects.

topics.name: Runtime memory protection: guard pages, fat pointers, MTE
topics.key_points: MMU: page tables map virtual→physical + permissions; MPU maps physical regions to permissions. Guard pages: MMU-illegal pages placed between stack frames/heap buffers/critical regions; any access aborts. Fat pointers carry key+base+bound; allocation generates random key, dereference checks key match, free rotates key. ARM MTE: 4-bit tag per 16-byte granule, pointer tag in bits 59–56, HW checks tag on access.

topics.name: Control-flow integrity defenses
topics.key_points: Goal: prevent/detect altered control flow (return pointer or function pointer modification). Stack canaries: random per-execution value between locals and saved FP/return addr; abort if changed (GCC -fstack-protector). Shadow stack: return addresses in separate guard-page-protected stack, compared on return; protects returns only, not other pointers/data. Target address encryption (XOR keyed pointers; XOR noted as weak). Control-flow attestation: log PC updates via trampoline invoke(), hash in isolated memory for verifier.

topics.name: Code integrity: W⊕X, signatures, ISR
topics.key_points: Prevent code injection/overwriting. W⊕X (NX): stack/heap/global data non-executable via MMU; needs JIT provisions (mprotect) — attacker can corrupt control flow to call mprotect then execute (see ROP). Code signatures: check SHA(program) in DB or verify DecMSpu(signature)=SHA(program) via certificate chain; runtime variant checks pages as they become executable; also malware-fragment DB. Instruction Set Randomization: encrypt code in memory, decrypt on fetch; injected code decrypts unpredictably. Requires cheap tweakable encryption preserving length, random access, no OFB/MAC.

topics.name: Disk encryption
topics.key_points: Use symmetric encryption (not asymmetric) for disks. AES-ECB is insecure (leaks patterns); CBC unsuitable due to random-access needs. Use tweakable encryption (per-sector tweak); add a MAC if integrity is required.

topics.name: Defense guarantees & remaining attacks
topics.key_points: Memory-safe languages: prevent invalid access in safe code; remain vulnerable to logic errors, side channels, unsafe bugs. Stack canary: detects canary change; fails on disclosure/bypass writes. W⊕X: blocks W+X mappings; ROP/data-only attacks remain. ASLR: unpredictability; fails on leaks/guessing. CFI/shadow stack: restricts indirect targets; abuse of allowed targets remains. Isolation/sandbox: limits compromised components; interface bugs and escapes remain.

topics.name: Block Ciphers & AES
topics.key_points: Block cipher: E(K,M)->C maps k-bit key + n-bit plaintext to n-bit ciphertext; D is inverse. Correctness: E_K must be a permutation (bijective). Security: E behaves like a random permutation, formalized via a distinguishing game (Eve can't tell E_K from random permutation with prob >1/2). Brute-forcing 128-bit key ~2^128≈10^39 keys ≈ 30 trillion years at 10^18 keys/s. AES: block 128 bits, keys 128/192/256 bits; 10/12/14 rounds (SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey).

topics.name: Limitations of Block Ciphers
topics.key_points: Block ciphers are NOT IND-CPA secure because deterministic: Eve submits M0,M1, re-requests Enc(K,M0) and compares — wins with probability 1. No deterministic scheme can be IND-CPA secure. Also, they only encrypt fixed n-bit blocks (AES: 128 bits); longer messages need modes of operation (covered in Lecture 5).

topics.name: Cryptographic Hash Functions
topics.key_points: H: {0,1}* -> {0,1}^n; fixed-length 'fingerprint'. Properties: deterministic, efficient, one-way (preimage resistance: given y, infeasible to find x with H(x)=y), collision resistance. Strong collision resistance (find any x≠x' with H(x)=H(x')) implies second preimage (weak) resistance (given x, find x'≠x colliding). Collisions must exist by pigeonhole; goal is computational infeasibility. Random oracle: 1-bit input change fully changes output.

topics.name: Hash Standards & Length Extension
topics.key_points: MD5 (128-bit, completely broken), SHA-1 (160-bit, broken 2017), SHA-2 (256/384/512, current standard but some variants vulnerable to length extension), SHA-3 (256/384/512, different construction, not vulnerable). Length extension: given H(x) and len(x) but not x, attacker can compute H(x||m) for chosen m.

topics.name: Hashes and Integrity (Threat Models)
topics.key_points: Hashes give integrity only if attacker can't modify the hash (e.g. Mozilla publishes hash on website; Alice compares). Over an insecure channel where Mallory can alter both message and hash, no integrity: hashes are unkeyed, anyone can compute them. Fix: keyed schemes (MACs) in symmetric setting.

topics.name: MACs, EU-CPA, NMAC & HMAC
topics.key_points: MAC(K,M)->T: key + arbitrary message to fixed tag. Security: EU-CPA (existential unforgeability under chosen-plaintext attack): even querying tags for chosen messages, Mallory can't forge a valid tag for a new M'. NMAC: H(K1||H(K2||M)), needs two n-bit keys; double hashing blocks length extension. HMAC: H((K'⊕opad)||H((K'⊕ipad)||M)); K' padded/hashed to n bits; opad=0x5c..., ipad=0x36... MACs give integrity/authenticity but NO confidentiality (deterministic, may leak info).

topics.name: Authenticated Encryption
topics.key_points: AE = confidentiality + integrity (+authenticity) simultaneously. Built by combining IND-CPA encryption with unforgeable MAC. Options: MAC-then-encrypt Enc(K1, M||MAC(K2,M)) vs encrypt-then-MAC Enc(K1,M) with MAC(K2, Enc(K1,M)). Both secure in theory, but always use encrypt-then-MAC: tampering detected before decryption, avoids feeding attacker-chosen input to decryption (side-channel leaks).

topics.name: Public-Key Encryption & Digital Signatures
topics.key_points: PKE: KeyGen()->PK,SK; Enc(PK,M)->C; Dec(SK,C)->M. Anyone encrypts with PK, only SK holder decrypts. Security: semantic security (IND-CPA variant where adversary gets PK). Examples: RSA, ElGamal (hardness of factorization/discrete log). Digital signatures: asymmetric integrity/authenticity, no shared key needed. Sign(SK,M)->sig; Verify(PK,M,sig)->{0,1}; only SK holder signs, anyone verifies. Security: EU-CPA as for MACs. In practice sign H(M) to handle long messages.

topics.name: What is social engineering & why it matters
topics.key_points: Attacks exploiting human behavior, not system vulnerabilities. Many/most attacks start via social engineering or human error (entry point). Goals: industrial spying, direct/indirect access to resources (trend: ransomware), data theft, identity theft. Everyone is susceptible. Reference: Kevin Mitnick, The Art of Deception / The Art of Intrusion.

topics.name: Why we fall for it
topics.key_points: Manipulation strategies exploit human traits, habits, cultural expectations. Unrealistic assumptions: 'I'm not important enough to be a target' (but you can be a stepping stone), 'this info isn't harmful if leaked' (but it can be combined), 'saying no creates problems', 'getting phished reflects on my intelligence' (it reflects on humanity and attacker manipulativeness). Tech advances make fake hard to distinguish from real.

topics.name: Attack phases
topics.key_points: 1) Research. 2) Pretexting — develop rapport and trust. 3) Get data (exploit trust). 4) Keep connections. 5) Combine data. 6) Use it. Small pieces from different sources are aggregated into a complete picture.

topics.name: Social engineering techniques
topics.key_points: Trappings of role; building credibility; altercasting (forcing the target into a role); distracting from systematic thinking; momentum of compliance; bury questions; get pieces from different sources. Also: read victim's openness, test with personal information, back off (don't burn the source), create then fix a problem to build gratitude/trust.

topics.name: Psychological exploits
topics.key_points: Levers the social engineer exploits: the desire to help, attribution, liking, fear, reactance (resistance to perceived loss of freedom), reciprocity, and the dynamics of doing a favor. Same persuasive techniques used in everyday life, applied manipulatively and deceptively (Brad Sagan quote).

topics.name: Example scenarios (Mitnick)
topics.key_points: Vishing (crying-baby call). 'Flying out': fake travel agency extracts employee number via friendly pretext. 'Just testing': fake tech support has victim change password to 'test123' during a bogus keystroke test. 'Network outage': multi-call attack — rapport with victim, trick NOC into disabling victim's port, victim calls attacker back for 'help', then is walked through downloading malware.

topics.name: Technical methods aiding SE
topics.key_points: Browser-in-the-Browser popups (Steam example); look-alike subdomains (www.microsoft.com.<junk>.reallybaddomain.com); deepfakes; HTML canvas + JavaScript + images to fake websites — last-mile reassembly attack for social engineering. Technology makes fake increasingly indistinguishable from real.

topics.name: Countermeasures
topics.key_points: Organizational: clear concise enforced protocols; awareness training dispelling myths; simple rules defining sensitive info; ID required for restricted actions; data classification policy; resistance training; security assessment testing (without setting traps); culture change — politeness where 'NO' is OK. Technical: filter phishing before it reaches users, 2FA, least privilege, isolation, separation of duty, complete mediation, patching.
